questions.q: In the lab's 2-marked-item oracle (marking indices 1 and 3 out of N=4), why is a single Z gate on qs[1] sufficient to mark both items?
options: Z gates always mark every state in the register regardless of qubit value
Both marked indices (1 and 3) share the same value (One) on the low-order qubit, so a Z on just that qubit flips the sign of both of them simultaneously
Z gates can only be applied to even-indexed states
It is not actually sufficient; the example in the lesson is incorrect
questions.explain: Indices 1 (|01>) and 3 (|11>) both have qs[1]=One; Z only affects the |1> component, so applying it to qs[1] alone flips the sign on exactly those two basis states.

questions.q: What was the verified exact result of running one Grover iteration with 2 marked items out of 4?
options: Probability 1.0 on both marked items
Probability exactly 0.25 on all four items -- identical to the starting uniform distribution, meaning zero net amplification
Probability 0 on all four items
Probability 0.5 on each marked item and 0 on each unmarked item
questions.explain: Direct matrix computation showed the inner product driving the diffusion step was exactly zero in this case, leaving the final probabilities at [0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25] -- identical to the uniform starting state.

questions.q: Mathematically, why did one Grover iteration produce no amplification at all in the 2-marked-item case?
options: Because Grover's algorithm never works with more than one marked item

Because the diffusion operator's effect scales with the inner product between the uniform superposition and the oracle's output state, and with exactly half the search space marked, that inner product canceled exactly to zero
Because the qubits were not properly entangled
Because Z gates have no mathematical effect on superpositions
questions.explain: The diffusion reflection depends on <s|oracle_state>; with 2 of 4 items marked, the positive and negative contributions to that inner product canceled exactly, producing D*v = -v, i.e. a sign flip with no change in probabilities.

questions.q: What general lesson does this exercise demonstrate about choosing the number of Grover iterations?
options: More marked items always means the search gets easier with fewer iterations needed

The correct number of iterations depends on both N and the actual number of marked items M (roughly pi/4 x sqrt(N/M)); reusing an iteration count tuned for a different M can produce zero improvement over random guessing
The number of iterations never matters as long as at least one item is marked
Diffusion operators should never be applied more than once regardless of M
questions.explain: This exercise is a concrete demonstration that getting M wrong (or assuming a fixed iteration count) can leave you with no advantage at all -- the optimal iteration count genuinely depends on M, not just N.

questions.q: What is a genuine practical limitation of Grover's algorithm that this exercise points toward?
options: Grover's algorithm requires measuring qubits before applying any gates
You generally need to know (or estimate) the number of marked items M in advance to choose a good iteration count, since guessing wrong can eliminate any amplification benefit
Grover's algorithm cannot be implemented in Q# at all
Diffusion operators only work correctly when N is odd
questions.explain: Since the optimal iteration count depends on M, and this exercise shows a wrong assumption about M can produce zero benefit, knowing or estimating M in advance is a real practical requirement for using Grover's algorithm effectively.
